title: SP$^2$ec: Adaptive Self-Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
claim: A bandit-style selector picks a different draft configuration per input using acceptance and timing feedback, because the best configuration varies by input.
layout: 2 stacked rows, left-to-right flow, left inset plot, feedback loops under each row
description: The figure has a left inset titled 'Best drafter varies by prompt'. It plots speed against number of components, with a solid blue curve for Prompt A peaking at Q2 and a dashed orange curve for Prompt B peaking at Q3. To its right are two horizontal rows, one per prompt. Prompt A is a red ball image and Prompt B is a blue car image, each with a question-mark bubble. Each image feeds a purple SP²EC box labelled 'Choose a drafter', which shows three striped-bar drafters Q1, Q2 and Q3. The chosen drafter is highlighted in blue for A (Q2) and orange for B (Q3). The flow then goes through Draft tokens, a blue Target model verify block, and Output tokens with green check marks and red strikethroughs for rejected tokens. A purple feedback arrow labelled 'Accepted tokens + time' returns to the drafter selector.
caption: Prompt-level adaptive drafter selection in SP2EC. Each arm corresponds to a drafter with different layer-skipping configuration and wall-time cost. SP2EC uses accepted-token and time feedback from the target model to exploit the single-peak throughput structure and adaptively select a drafter during generation. Different prompts can favor different arms, motivating per-query adaptation for VLM speculative decoding.
abstract: Speculative Decoding (SD) has demonstrated its efficacy in accelerating large language model inference, but for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), the diverse input modalities make it difficult for a small trained drafter to achieve consistently high throughput. Self-speculative decoding reuses parts of the target model as a drafter which retains the multi-modal capability of the VLMs, yet its efficiency depends on choosing a suitable draft configuration for each prompt. We propose Single-Peak SPeculative decoding (SP$^2$ec), a training-free bandit algorithm that adapts the draft configuration during generation. SP$^2$ec exploits the single-peak throughput pattern observed in existing self-speculative methods, including SWIFT, KnapSpec, SpecVLM, and our simple cosSim. Our algorithmic design explicitly minimizes a novel notion of wall-time regret for each given query, corresponding to the empirical wall-time latency. Theoretical guarantees on the wall-time regret show that SP$^2$ec can exploit the optimal draft configuration, with negligible exploration cost. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B across visual and textual tasks show consistent improvements of up to 11% over the original self-speculative methods, demonstrating the wide applicability of the proposed SP$^2$ec algorithm.
